transcript.text:
Let's narrow it down. First, what exactly do you see?

• Completely black, no lights at all → likely a power issue
• Black screen but you hear sound → backlight or display issue
• "No Signal" message → input/source or cable issue
• Standby light on but nothing happens → TV is stuck or not waking up

## Quick fixes to try first

1. Power cycle (fixes most problems)
• Unplug the TV from the wall (not just the remote off).
• Wait 60 seconds. Optionally hold the TV's physical power button for 15 to 30 seconds while unplugged.
• Plug it back in and turn it on.

2. Check the input/source
• Press Input or Source on the remote and cycle through the inputs (HDMI 1, HDMI 2, TV, etc.).
• Make sure the device you're using (cable box, Roku, console) is turned on.

3. Check cables
• Unplug and firmly reconnect the HDMI cable at both ends.
• Try a different HDMI port or a different cable.
• Make sure the power cord is snug in the back of the TV.

4. Try the TV's own menu
• Press Menu or Home. If the menu appears, the TV works and the problem is the connected device or cable.

5. Check the remote
• Replace the batteries, or use the power button on the TV itself.

## Flashlight test (if you hear sound but see black)

Shine a flashlight close to the screen at an angle with the TV on. If you can faintly see images, the backlight has failed. This is a common hardware fault that usually needs repair.

## Blinking standby light

If the red or white light blinks in a pattern, that's an error code. Count the blinks and look it up for your brand.

---

Let me know:
• TV brand and model (e.g., Samsung, LG, TCL, Vizio)
• What you see and hear
• What you're watching through (cable box, streaming stick, antenna, built-in apps)

With that, I can give you more specific steps.

That points to either a setting that turned the screen off or a backlight failure. Here's how to tell which.

## Step 1: Rule out the simple stuff

Press Menu or Home on the remote.
• Menu shows up → The TV's screen works. The problem is your source device or cable. Reseat or swap the HDMI cable and restart the device.
• Still black → Continue below.

Check for a "screen off" setting. Many TVs can turn off the picture while keeping audio playing, often triggered by accident.
• Press any button (volume, input, power briefly) to see if the picture returns.
• Look for settings like Screen Off, Picture Off, Energy Saving, or Eco Mode. Set energy saving to Off or Low.
• If brightness or backlight was set to 0, that can also cause this.

Power cycle it. Unplug from the wall for 60 seconds, then plug back in.

## Step 2: Flashlight test

1. Turn the TV on with something playing, or press Menu.
2. Shine a phone flashlight close to the screen at an angle.
3. Look carefully for faint images or menu text.

You see a faint picture → The backlight has failed. The screen and electronics work, but the LEDs behind the panel are out. This is very common, especially on LED TVs a few years old.

You see nothing at all → It's more likely a problem with the T-con board, main board, or panel. That's harder to diagnose without the model number.

## If it's the backlight

• Under warranty? Check the receipt or the manufacturer's site with your serial number. Contact them first.
• Repair shop: Usually costs about $100 to $200. That's worth it for a larger or newer TV. It may not be worth it for a cheap or small one.
• DIY: Replacement LED strips are sold online for most models (search your model number + "LED backlight strips"). It's doable but involves taking the panel apart carefully, and it's easy to crack the screen. Only try it if you're comfortable with that.
• Replace: For an older budget TV, a new one may cost about the same as the repair.

---

What happened with the Menu button and the flashlight test? If you share the brand and model, I can point you to the exact settings or common faults for that TV.

The problem is in the TV itself, not your cable box or streaming device. It's either a hidden setting or a hardware fault. These steps will tell you which.

## 1. Power cycle
If you haven't yet: unplug the TV from the wall, hold the TV's physical power button for 30 seconds, wait a full minute, then plug it back in. This clears temporary glitches.

## 2. Flashlight test (the key step)
1. Turn the TV on and press Home so the menu is "up."
2. In a dim room, hold your phone flashlight an inch or two from the screen, angled slightly.
3. Look closely for faint menu icons or text.

Faint image visible → Backlight failure (most likely cause).
Nothing at all → Possibly the T-con board, main board, or panel.

## 3. Check for a "picture off" setting using your phone
Since you can't see the menu, use your brand's phone app as a remote to turn off any setting that blanks the screen:
• Samsung: SmartThings
• LG: LG ThinQ
• Roku TVs (TCL, Hisense, etc.): Roku app
• Google TV / Android TV (Sony, TCL, Hisense): Google Home or Google TV app
• Vizio: Vizio Mobile / SmartCast

In the app, look for Picture Off, Screen Off, or Energy Saving, and set backlight/brightness to a normal level. If the picture comes back, you're done.

## 4. Watch the standby light
After a power cycle, see if the light blinks in a pattern. Blink codes point to specific failed parts.

---

Tell me:
• What did the flashlight test show?
• Brand and model number (on a sticker on the back of the TV)
• Roughly how old is the TV?

With that, I can tell you whether it's likely worth repairing and what to expect.
Torch test: I can just see the menu faintly where the torch shines.

That confirms it: the backlight has failed. The TV's electronics and screen are working, but the LEDs that light the panel from behind aren't. This is one of the most common TV faults, and it's usually fixable.

## One last check before paying for anything
Make sure it isn't just a setting. Use your brand's phone app (SmartThings, LG ThinQ, Roku, Google TV, etc.) to confirm Backlight/Brightness isn't at 0 and Energy Saving / Picture Off is turned off. It's rare, but it costs nothing to rule out.

## Your options

1. Warranty or consumer rights (check first)
• Check the manufacturer's warranty with your serial number.
• In the UK, the Consumer Rights Act lets you claim against the retailer for faults that were likely present from manufacture, for up to 6 years (5 in Scotland). Backlight failure in a TV only a few years old is often accepted. In the first 6 months, the retailer must assume the fault was there from the start.
• Some retailers (e.g., John Lewis) include longer guarantees, and some home insurance or bank accounts cover appliances.

2. Professional repair (about £80 to £200)
• A local TV repair shop replaces the LED strips. This is usually worth it for TVs over about 43" or less than 5 years old.
• Ask for a quote first and check they use quality strips, since cheap ones can fail again.

3. DIY (about £15 to £50 for parts)
• Search your model number + "LED backlight strips" on eBay or AliExpress.
• You have to remove the back, lift out the panel and diffuser layers, and swap the strips. It's very doable with patience and a YouTube guide for your model, but the panel cracks easily, so you need a clean, flat space and ideally a second person.
• Replace all the strips, not just the dead one, since the rest are likely near failure too.

4. Replace the TV
For a small or older budget TV, a new one may cost about the same as a repair.

## Meanwhile
Keep using it for audio if you like, but avoid running it for long periods. A failed strip can sometimes stress the power board.

---

If you share the brand, model number, and screen size, I can tell you whether it's a known issue for that model, roughly what parts cost, and whether repair is worth it.
its a Samsung UE55TU7100KXXU, about 5 years old. i won't take the back off though

Thanks, that helps. The UE55TU7100 is a 2020 Samsung 55" 4K model, and backlight failure is a fairly commonly reported fault on this series. Since you don't want to open it yourself, here's what I'd do, in order.

## 1. Try a claim under the Consumer Rights Act (free if it works)
At about 5 years old, you're still within the 6-year limit (5 in Scotland).
• Contact the retailer you bought it from, not Samsung. Your contract is with them.
• Say the TV has a backlight fault and you believe it was not of satisfactory quality or durability, since a mid-range 55" TV should reasonably last longer than 5 years.
• After the first 6 months, it's up to you to show the fault was inherent. Retailers may ask for a repair report, which a local shop can provide (sometimes for a small fee, or free if they do the repair).
• Don't expect a full refund at this age. A free repair or a partial refund, reduced for the years of use, is more realistic.
• Have your proof of purchase (receipt, bank statement, or online order history) ready.

Also check whether you have cover through home insurance, a packaged bank account, or an extended warranty bought with the TV.

## 2. Get a repair quote
The manufacturer's warranty will have expired, so a local independent TV repair shop is usually the cheapest route.
• Expect roughly £90 to £180 for this model. Replacement strips for the TU7100 are cheap and widely available, so most of the cost is labour.
• Many shops do home visits or collection, which is handy for a 55".
• Ask them to:
• Replace all the LED strips, not just the failed one, since the rest are the same age and likely to fail soon too.
• Lower the backlight drive current if possible. Many repairers do this to make the new strips last longer, at the cost of a little brightness.
• Give a warranty on the repair (3 to 12 months is typical).

Samsung's own out-of-warranty repair service is an option, but it's usually more expensive than an independent shop.

## 3. Decide: repair or replace
A new 55" 4K TV costs roughly £300 to £450 depending on brand.
• Quote under about £150: repair. The rest of your TV works fine, and you'll likely get several more years from it.
• Quote over about £200: replacing it starts to make more sense, especially since a new TV comes with a fresh warranty and newer smart features.

## Meanwhile
It's fine to keep using the TV for audio. Running it won't do any real further damage.

If you'd like, I can help you word a message to the retailer for the Consumer Rights Act claim.
